title: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition) · Units 51–52
description: Advanced vocabulary for healthcare professionals, the British healthcare system, everyday illness, discomfort and recovery, with original examples, usage contrasts and Brazilian Portuguese meanings.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-provided book for personal study. The vocabulary selection follows the teaching pages and relevant exercise targets; translations, explanations and example sentences are newly written. Original book exercises, illustrations and extended passages are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Complete teaching and exercise pages for Units 51–52, including illustrations, UK healthcare terminology, language help and answer-key entries for exercises 51.1–51.3 and 52.1–52.4.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA is supplied conservatively for short targets with reliable forms; longer or uncertain expressions have empty IPA. The package does not attempt connected-speech or accent-variant transcription.
audit.languagePolicy: All learner-facing English fields and metadata are in English; Brazilian Portuguese is used only in pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Compared teaching pages, text and illustrations, exercises and the relevant answer key. Reviewed lexical coverage, UK institutional terms, medical/lay distinctions, collocations, translations and independently written examples; performed static schema, uniqueness and TTS-target validation.
audit.limitations: No MP3 files are bundled. Importing into the real VocabLab UI, browser TTS quality and speech recognition have not been tested. UK health-system descriptions reflect the textbook context and may vary by UK nation and over time. The descriptive vocabulary for non-conventional therapies is not an endorsement of effectiveness.

units.title: Unit 51 — Healthcare
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 108–109 (PDF pages 110–111).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: Health and medicine · professionals and healthcare systems
learningObjectives: Distinguish first-contact primary care from specialist secondary care and describe referral patterns.
Use British healthcare terminology, including GP, locum, surgery, NHS and prescription charges, with attention to local variation.
Identify medical specialists and their fields without confusing healthcare roles.
Recognise alternative and complementary medicine as descriptive categories without assuming efficacy.

Figures, language-help/usage contrasts and all exercise questions
Exercises and corresponding answer-key entries for this unit

items.section: A · Healthcare professionals and levels of care
items.example: The clinic employs healthcare professionals from several different disciplines.
items.note: An umbrella term for qualified people involved in providing health services.

items.section: A · Healthcare professionals and levels of care
items.example: Patients usually enter the health system through primary care.
items.note: First-contact medical care, typically offered by general practitioners and nurses.

items.pt: atenção secundária à saúde; atendimento especializado
items.section: A · Healthcare professionals and levels of care
items.example: The family doctor referred her to secondary care for further investigation.
items.note: Specialist care generally provided in clinics or hospitals following referral.

items.pt: sistema de atenção primária à saúde
items.section: A · Healthcare professionals and levels of care
items.example: A strong primary care system helps coordinate patients' treatment over time.
items.note: The network of first-contact health services, as distinct from specialist services.

items.section: A · Healthcare professionals and levels of care
items.example: The physician reviewed the results before discussing further tests.
items.note: A formal term for a medical doctor, particularly common in American usage.

items.section: A · Healthcare professionals and levels of care
items.example: A nurse explained how the appointment system worked.
items.note: A healthcare professional trained in nursing; often works in primary and secondary care.

items.pt: consultório médico; unidade de atendimento de clínico geral
items.section: A · Healthcare professionals and levels of care
items.example: I called the doctor's surgery to arrange a routine appointment.
items.note: In British English, surgery can mean a GP's consulting premises as well as an operation.

items.pt: visita domiciliar de profissional de saúde
items.section: A · Healthcare professionals and levels of care
items.example: The practice arranged a home visit for a patient unable to travel.
items.note: A visit by a doctor or another healthcare professional to a patient's home.

items.pt: médico substituto; profissional de saúde temporário
items.section: A · Healthcare professionals and levels of care
items.example: The practice hired a locum while the usual GP was on leave.
items.note: In this unit, a doctor temporarily replacing another doctor; the term can also apply to other professions.

items.pt: condição aguda; problema de saúde de início súbito
items.section: A · Healthcare professionals and levels of care
items.example: The clinic has a separate pathway for patients with an acute condition.
items.note: Acute describes sudden onset and often marked severity; it does not necessarily mean short-term or minor.

items.pt: condição crônica; problema de saúde persistente
items.section: A · Healthcare professionals and levels of care
items.example: A chronic condition may require long-term follow-up.
items.note: Chronic means long-lasting or recurrent, not necessarily immediately severe.

items.word: refer a patient to a specialist
items.pt: encaminhar um paciente a um especialista
items.section: A · Healthcare professionals and levels of care
items.example: The GP decided to refer the patient to a specialist for assessment.
items.note: Pattern: refer someone to someone; a referral is the corresponding noun.

items.section: A · Healthcare professionals and levels of care
items.example: She hopes to specialise in paediatric medicine.
items.note: British spelling; follow specialise with in plus a field or condition.

items.section: A · Healthcare professionals and levels of care
items.example: The surgeon checked that the organ was functioning normally.
items.note: A body part with a specific function, such as the heart or liver.

items.section: A · Healthcare professionals and levels of care
items.example: An ophthalmologist examined his eyes after the injury.
items.note: Medical specialist concerned with eyes and eye diseases.

items.section: A · Healthcare professionals and levels of care
items.example: The cardiologist discussed the patient's test results with the GP.
items.note: Medical specialist concerned with the heart.

items.section: A · Healthcare professionals and levels of care
items.example: A psychiatrist may work as part of a multidisciplinary clinical team.
items.note: Medical doctor specialising in mental health and psychiatric treatment.

items.section: A · Healthcare professionals and levels of care
items.example: A dermatologist assessed the persistent skin problem.
items.note: Medical specialist concerned with the skin.

items.section: A · Healthcare professionals and levels of care
items.example: The gynaecologist works in a women's health clinic.
items.note: British spelling; medical specialist in the female reproductive system.

items.section: A · Healthcare professionals and levels of care
items.example: The obstetrician coordinated care during the final weeks of pregnancy.
items.note: Medical specialist in pregnancy and childbirth.

items.section: A · Healthcare professionals and levels of care
items.example: The child was seen by a paediatrician at the hospital.
items.note: British spelling; doctor specialising in children's health.

items.section: A · Healthcare professionals and levels of care
items.example: The anaesthetist discussed the procedure with the patient beforehand.
items.note: British English term for a doctor specialising in anaesthesia.

items.section: A · Healthcare professionals and levels of care
items.example: The patient was given anaesthesia before the operation.
items.note: Loss or prevention of sensation, commonly used during medical procedures.

items.example: The article compared claims made by providers of alternative medicine.
items.note: The term describes approaches outside conventional medicine; the label itself does not establish clinical effectiveness.

items.example: The hospital discussed how complementary medicine differs from its standard treatments.
items.note: Refers to non-conventional approaches used alongside standard care, rather than instead of it.

items.example: She interviewed an acupuncturist for her research on health services.
items.note: A practitioner of acupuncture, an approach using needles at selected points on the body.

items.example: The documentary interviewed a chiropractor about their professional training.
items.note: Practitioner associated with manual treatment focused especially on joints and the spine.

items.example: The survey asked respondents whether they had consulted a homeopathic doctor.
items.note: A practitioner of homeopathy, a non-conventional approach described in the source; the term does not establish clinical effectiveness.

items.example: The centre employed an aromatherapist offering scented-oil massage.
items.note: A practitioner using aromatic oils, often with massage; avoid assuming a medical treatment benefit.

items.pt: assistência à saúde; serviços de saúde
items.example: Access to healthcare is a major issue in public policy.
items.note: The broad range of services provided by medical and related professionals.

items.example: The payslip listed deductions for tax and National Insurance.
items.note: UK social-insurance contributions; the book discusses them in relation to financing public services.

items.pt: Serviço Nacional de Saúde do Reino Unido
items.example: The National Health Service provides a wide range of publicly funded care.
items.note: Official name of the UK's publicly funded healthcare services, often shortened to NHS.

items.pt: sigla de National Health Service; sistema público de saúde britânico
items.example: The report examined staffing pressures across the NHS.
items.note: Initialism read letter by letter: N-H-S; it refers to the UK public health services.

items.example: A general practitioner assessed the problem before arranging a referral.
items.note: Commonly abbreviated to GP in Britain; a doctor providing first-contact care.

items.example: Her GP recommended arranging an appointment with a specialist.
items.note: Initialism for general practitioner, read as two letters, G-P.

items.example: The family doctor reviewed the patient's history during the consultation.
items.note: A doctor providing ongoing general care; a natural alternative to GP in many contexts.

items.example: The specialist clinic accepts referrals from local GP practices.
items.note: A centre that provides particular healthcare services or treatments.

items.example: The brochure explained who was exempt from the prescription charge.
items.note: A fee for prescribed medicine; exemptions and rules vary across UK nations and over time.

items.example: The doctor issued a prescription following the consultation.
items.note: The written or electronic instruction authorising a medicine; not the medicine itself.

items.example: She collected the prescribed medicine from the pharmacy.
items.note: A place where prescribed medicines are dispensed.

items.pt: assistência médica privada; serviços privados de saúde
items.example: Some employees receive private healthcare through their employer.
items.note: Healthcare paid for privately or through private insurance rather than public provision.

items.example: The company offers an insurance scheme that covers selected medical services.
items.note: An organised insurance arrangement, often with specified limits and exclusions.

items.pt: optar pelo atendimento privado de saúde
items.example: After comparing the options, he decided to go private for the consultation.
items.note: British expression meaning choose private healthcare rather than public provision.

units.title: Unit 52 — Illness: feeling under the weather
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 110–111 (PDF pages 112–113).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: Health and medicine · everyday illness and recovery
learningObjectives: Use informal expressions for feeling unwell and distinguish coming down with an illness from suffering from a long-term condition.
Differentiate hurt, ache, physical discomfort and emotional hurt in common collocations.
Describe minor symptoms and injuries naturally, including fixed-order expressions and British usage.
Distinguish being over the worst, on the mend and back on your feet as different stages of recovery.

sectionsChecked: Unit study sections, word meanings, UK usage and explanatory footnotes
Figures, language-help/usage contrasts and all exercise questions
Exercises and corresponding answer-key entries for this unit

items.example: She looked slightly off-colour during the morning meeting.
items.note: Informal British expression for appearing or feeling mildly unwell.

items.pt: indisposto; meio estranho; fora de si
items.example: I've been feeling out of sorts since the long journey.
items.note: Idiomatic, rather informal way of saying you do not feel your usual self.

items.example: He stayed home because he felt under the weather.
items.note: Informal fixed phrase usually describing mild illness.

items.example: The child had been feeling poorly for several days.
items.note: Informal, especially British, adjective meaning unwell; not the adverb sense of badly.

items.pt: combater um resfriado; tentar se livrar de um resfriado
items.example: I'm trying to fight off a cold before the conference.
items.note: Fight off means resist or recover from an illness; it can express an effort or success.

items.example: Several members of the team went down with flu last winter.
items.note: In the book, go down with is especially common when talking about other people.

items.example: I think I'm coming down with a cold, so I'll rest this evening.
items.note: Come down with means begin to suffer from an illness; the book prefers this for your own illness.

items.pt: sofrer de; ter um problema de saúde
items.example: She has suffered from hay fever since childhood.
items.note: Pattern: suffer from a disease or long-term problem, not suffer of.

items.pt: rinite alérgica sazonal; alergia a pólen
items.example: His hay fever gets worse during the spring pollen season.
items.note: Seasonal allergic symptoms often triggered by airborne pollen.

items.example: She began to sneeze after walking through the garden.
items.note: Verb for involuntarily expelling air through the nose and mouth.

items.example: My wrist hurts when I try to lift the box.
items.note: In this contrast, hurt is a verb describing pain, often associated with injury.

items.example: My shoulders ache after working at the desk all day.
items.note: A verb or noun often describing persistent, less sharp pain.

items.example: He developed backache after carrying heavy equipment.
items.note: Compound noun commonly used without an article: have backache.

items.example: Apart from the usual aches and pains, he felt reasonably well.
items.note: Fixed sequence describing minor bodily discomforts; not pains and aches.

items.example: The cyclist escaped with a few cuts and bruises.
items.note: Fixed order for relatively minor injuries, not bruises and cuts.

items.pt: arder; causar sensação de queimação ou picada
items.example: The scratch began to sting when she washed it.
items.note: A sharp or burning sensation; as a verb its past tense is stung.

items.example: His injured finger continued to throb throughout the evening.
items.note: Describes rhythmic, pulsating pain.

items.example: She woke up with a stiff neck after sleeping awkwardly.
items.note: Stiff means difficult or painful to move, not necessarily damaged.

items.example: You could twist your ankle on that uneven path.
items.note: Twist an ankle or knee means injure it by turning it suddenly.

items.example: He felt dizzy after standing up too quickly.
items.note: Feeling that you or the surroundings are spinning, or that balance is affected.

items.example: She felt feverish and decided to check her temperature.
items.note: Having or feeling as though you have a fever.

items.example: She felt shivery even though the room was warm.
items.note: Shaking or feeling cold, sometimes associated with a fever.

items.pt: alternar sensações de calor e frio; sentir calafrios
items.example: He was feeling hot and cold during the night.
items.note: Everyday expression for fluctuating sensations often associated with illness.

items.example: She stayed home because she had a temperature.
items.note: British English phrase meaning have a fever, not simply own a thermometer.

items.pt: noite em claro; noite sem dormir
items.example: The noise outside caused another sleepless night.
items.note: A night with little or no sleep; sleepless describes the night.

items.example: The smell inside the bus made him feel nauseous.
items.note: Feeling as if you might vomit; often followed by feel.

items.example: Her hands began to tremble after she came in from the cold.
items.note: To shake slightly, for example with cold, fear or illness.

items.example: My nose is completely bunged up this morning.
items.note: Informal British expression for blocked nasal passages.

items.pt: dor surda; dor persistente e pouco intensa
items.section: B · Describing aches and emotional hurt
items.example: A dull ache remained in his shoulder after the journey.
items.note: Describes a steady pain that is not especially sharp.

items.section: B · Describing aches and emotional hurt
items.example: She mentioned a nagging ache that kept distracting her.
items.note: Nagging suggests a repeated, persistent and irritating sensation.

items.section: B · Describing aches and emotional hurt
items.example: He reported a throbbing ache around the injured toe.
items.note: Combines the noun ache with an adjective describing pulsating pain.

items.section: B · Describing aches and emotional hurt
items.example: The betrayal caused deep hurt within the family.
items.note: As a noun, hurt often refers to emotional pain, unlike the physical noun ache.

items.example: It took her several weeks to get over the infection.
items.note: Informal phrasal verb for recovering; get over can take other experiences as objects.

items.example: He is recovering from an operation at home.
items.note: The verb commonly takes from before the illness, injury or procedure.

items.example: He's on the mend, although he still gets tired quickly.
items.note: Means health is improving and recovery is in progress.

items.pt: já passou da fase mais grave
items.example: The doctors believed she was over the worst after the first few difficult days.
items.note: The most serious stage has passed, but the person may not yet be well.

items.pt: recuperado; de volta às atividades normais
items.example: After a long recovery, she was back on her feet again.
items.note: Usually suggests sufficiently good health to resume normal activity.

items.example: The questionnaire asked whether participants had any allergies.
items.note: Countable: an allergy to something; an allergic reaction is a related phrase.
